current_episode.title: PODCAST: IBEW/NECA's Sylvester Taylor on Designing a Welcoming Construction Workforce

guest.titre: Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Initiatives
guest.entreprise: The Electrical Connection (IBEW Local One and NECA St. Louis Chapter)
guest.bio_context: Sylvester Taylor has been an electrician with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers for 32 years. He is co-founder and president of the Electrical Workers Minority Caucus, and was appointed in March to lead the first-ever joint diversity, equity, and inclusion position created between IBEW Local One and the National Electrical Contractors Association in the country. He previously served as a representative for the 80th District in the Missouri House of Representatives from 2012 to 2019, and serves as treasurer on the Hazelwood School Board and chairman of the St. Louis County Fire Safety and Standards Commission.

pending_qa.q: How does the practice of counting minority workers on individual projects versus actual workforce diversification differ?
pending_qa.r: Taylor states that simply putting six people on a job to meet minority participation requirements solves the immediate problem but does not achieve real workforce diversification. Workers are often laid off after the project ends, meaning no lasting change occurs. He emphasizes that retention and ongoing opportunity, not just placement numbers, define true diversity.

pending_qa.q: What specific barriers prevent young people, particularly those from underserved communities, from entering electrical apprenticeships?
pending_qa.r: Taylor identifies multiple barriers: educational inequity (lack of advanced math skills required for the trade), lack of transportation, insufficient healthcare and childcare support, and historically 25 years of pushing college as the only pathway. He notes that the math portion of the apprenticeship is where the organization loses the most young men and women.

pending_qa.q: What is the strategy to embed electrical trade curriculum into high school mathematics to increase apprenticeship qualification rates?
pending_qa.r: Taylor explains that IBEW and NECA are working with high schools to teach their math curriculum alongside standard high school math. The vision is that if apprentices already possess the required math skills, fewer students will fail the apprenticeship math portion. They have identified a couple of pilot schools and are still developing the plan of attack with school districts and DESE.

pending_qa.q: How many apprentices can IBEW Local One accommodate annually, and how does that compare to current demand?
pending_qa.r: IBEW Local One can take approximately 80 apprentices per year, based on industry work cycles. In the earlier part of the year discussed, the union interviewed 700 kids interested in joining IBEW—a number Taylor had never seen before—demonstrating far exceeds capacity.

pending_qa.q: What does Taylor identify as the personal strategy that allowed him to survive and advance within a historically hostile construction trade environment?
pending_qa.r: Taylor states: 'I had to bite my tongue until it was my turn to swing. Okay. And then when it was my turn to swing, I swung as hard as I could.' He also emphasizes that he had to change himself rather than waiting for the industry to change, and then he worked to smooth the road for those coming behind him.

pending_qa.q: What concrete example demonstrates the impact of early career entry in the electrical trades on economic mobility?
pending_qa.r: Taylor describes a young man he helped enter the trade at age 18 who, by age 21, purchased his first house. Taylor notes that this achievement puts the young man 'light years ahead' of where Taylor himself was at 21, when he was not even thinking about homeownership.

pending_qa.q: How should contractors and unions approach hiring women and people of color to ensure genuine inclusion rather than superficial compliance?
pending_qa.r: Taylor argues that contractors must place women and people of color in supervisory positions, not just entry-level roles. He uses the example that when a middle-aged white man fails on a job, the company hires the next white man; people of color and women deserve the same opportunity to fail and be replaced by another from their group, not to be excluded entirely based on one person's failure.

pending_qa.q: What role do changing political leadership demographics play in motivating organized labor to address diversity in construction?
pending_qa.r: Taylor notes that for the first time in Missouri state history, the two economic engines of the state—St. Louis and Kansas City—are led by African-American mayors, and that school boards and other power brokers throughout the region are increasingly African-American-led. These power brokers are now demanding contractors be more diverse or lose market share, creating new incentives for organized labor to act.
